blocks.x: What's your name anyway? My name is Al Rose. Is that your full name? No, my full name is H.N. Alphonse Delarose Lascaux. My God. I thought it was E. Albert Rose for years. Well, I actually did use that name for years for complex reasons. Where were you born? I was born in New Orleans in a 2-0 infirmary on February 3rd, 1916. Makes me 59 years old today. Just,

I'm not taking anything in any particular order. Okay. Other than happy birthday. Thank you, Richard. Oh, I didn't tell you my name. My name is Dick Allen, commonly known as Richard. Enough of this feeble attempt at you, and I'm tired. I interviewed Russell last night. Two hours of tennis and one hour of interview with Russell. It's an hour and a half. What I did with Russell. That's the D-In for a whole day. Where have you been a disc jockey? Well, I

wouldn't exactly think of myself as a disc jockey. I did, of course, run the radio show Journeys Into Jazz, which began in 1946 in Philadelphia, and is now syndicated through Southern Illinois University Radio Network. And it's just a mini-series of programs about jazz and jazz musicians on which records are played for illustration. What station was this in Philadelphia? WFIL, ABC. They had a little Eastern network that covered a lot of ABC affiliates in the area, and I had a pretty big audience back in the 40s. What was WPEN? Was that station? WPEN was a radio station in Philadelphia too. I didn't do my show there, but I was a frequent guest on the station when they were the headquarters for the radio show called Jukebox Jury. I'm
trying to remember because it seemed to me that a few years ago we were looking at some copies of records. You made dubs. And the blanks came from WPEN. Could that be correct? Oh yes, because
they had the recording facilities to do it with. And they may have been records that I made up there with either Dan Burley or Fats Waller or Sammy Price. You recorded them? Yeah. I think
these were copies of 78's commercial issue, but I didn't know about this particular thing. Fats Waller, huh? Yeah. I'd never heard you mention much about Fats before. Well, it wasn't actually a

commercial session. I mean, we just happened to be up in the station. And we, as a matter of fact, it was on my birthday then, too. And the record opens with the Fats saying, this is for my boy Al, you know, happy birthday, and so on. What year would that be? Oh, this was about 1937. And was this before Journeys into Jazz started? Oh yes, that was substantially before Journeys into Jazz. That was ten years before Journeys into Jazz.
I'm beginning to get the picture on you. So you, your activities date back before being in the jazz business, date back before Journeys into Jazz? Oh yes.

My first actual public activity in jazz was when I ran a jazz concert for the American Newspaper Guild in Philadelphia at Mercantile Hall. And that was in 1936, in January of 1936. And it included Sidney Bechet and Sidney D. Paris, members of Jack Teagarden's band who were playing upstairs for dancing. That included Sterling Boze and Boze and Irving Fazola. And a local clarinet player by the name of Billy Kretschmer was there. As far as I know, this is the first actual concert ever held of authentic jazz in which people came to buy tickets and sit down to listen. Well, you couldn't have been too old then. I was twenty. Did that cause you any problems? Yeah, it did, because I looked a lot younger than I was. And, uh, but having left home as early as I did, I was already experienced in, in, uh, compensating for all those problems.
Oh. What about, did you, did you have any trouble, uh, getting in? Have I, didn't you tell me something about that once? Are you, people didn't recognize you as the producer?

Oh, yeah. I, um, uh, I particularly had written that thing about the time I was in Symphony Hall in Boston running a concert there. And, uh, I had gone out for a cup of coffee or sandwich or something. And on my way back in, uh, the guard wouldn't let me in because he assumed that I was a kid trying to crash it. And when I explained to him who I was, he didn't believe me. And at last I had to get them to call backstage and Muggsy Spank came out and identified me and we went in. How many journeys into jazz concerts were there? Uh, there were just short of two hundred. I think it was a hundred and ninety-six or a hundred and ninety-seven. The last of which was in Carbondale, Illinois in nineteen sixty-seven. Do you plan to do any more concert? No, I really, uh, I don't think I'll ever do another concert because I don't think I can ever reassemble the quality of music that I consider to be essential for the proper presentation of jazz.

Well, I can, uh, I put on a few things, uh, myself, and I find it very depressing. When you try to, even though people may be in the right idiom, I still don't think they understand it. I have the right attitude sometimes. They, I don't.

I think they're socially conditioned away from it. You see the circumstances that produced the jazz, uh, also produced a different, uh, psychological set. And, uh, jazz as I knew it when I was a kid in New Orleans was basically an ensemble art. Nobody knew the names of leaders. Nobody knew the names of individual musicians. You only knew the names of bands, and you followed bands. And, uh, you got accustomed to a sound. Uh, there was no, uh, substantial soloing. Uh, a solo was an eight-bar break. And, uh, uh, uh, uh, the musicians were much better developed harmonically and much better developed tonally. So that, uh, there was an actual sound, uh, uh, an abstract sound of the, uh, without even considering the music, but just the tonal sound of the jazz was entirely different from anything that I have heard in recent years. The sound of the band, uh, the sound of the individual? The sound of the individuals and the band, the horns, the, the development of the tone itself. Uh, I could best describe it possibly as a far more vocal tone than the tone that you get now, which is, uh, uh, a relatively mechanical tone. Mm-hm. I heard it in the street.

Well, I don't want to mention names in this, but I've had the experience of, say, working with Johnny Wiggs or Percy Humphrey at concerts. It's getting really off the subject of you, but it's your perception of the music and what perspective. And you can change one person, get rid of Wiggs in a band, say, for example. And the whole band is changing the whole attitude.

Of course it is. It's because of the fact that a trumpet player like Johnny Wiggs knows the role of the cornet in the jazz band. He understands the nature of the lead. And most musicians are thinking in terms of each of his own performance, you see. And he does not know anymore how to listen to the sound of a band. And I get the feeling that he doesn't even really enjoy the sound of the band particularly, but is only considering what he himself is doing. And this is something that is relatively new in New Orleans jazz. I mean, new in relation to my own frame of reference.
I feel that there's a loss of respect for the music and the audience both.
Yes, there's especially a loss of respect for the melodies themselves. Yeah.

Well, and they don't particularly want to play. The enthusiasm isn't there. And they must prefer to take a break rather than work hard and enjoy themselves. And it's become merely a job to some people. But that's neither here nor there.

Well, you've been with me when I've made records, and you've seen my own approach to that, and you're aware of the fact that my own requirements for making records are different from other people's, largely because I am demanding that ensemble sound, and I'm demanding musicians that can play it and work together in that way.
Well, it's the kind of thing that's really painful to even say or discuss, but I think it's a fact that we're going to find very few bands in the future that are bands.
I think so.
And you may find a lot of good soloists.
Oh, you'll find a lot of excellent musicians. Yeah. But it's like the difference between being a great novelist and a great typist.
Yeah. What about, uh, what's the first time you ever remember hearing jazz, either on records or live or whatever?

Well, of course it had to be live, because I can't remember any time when I didn't hear jazz. There was no way that you could grow up in the French Quarter and not hear jazz, just walking around in the street. And, uh, especially I remember, uh, when I was a kid, there were so many skiffle bands playing in the streets, there were people to throw them coins, you know. And, uh, that was the sound. That was the, and of course I used to go down by the Fern Dance Hall and stand across the street and listen to the band playing for the Diamond Dance operation that they had going there. And that was when I first met Armand Hug. I was seven, he was fifteen. He was playing on the job, though.
So you were, uh, you were wandering around in the, uh, in the quarter. Where did you live in the corner?
On the corner of St. Louis and Dauphin. Sam Morgan might have been on your neighborhood.
Maybe, uh, although I wasn't aware of him. Yeah.
The very first thing I actually remembered as a dramatic incident was looking out the third story back window of the house and watching the French Opera burn.
Well, do you remember musicians that lived in the neighborhood down there?

I remember Danny Barker, although I didn't know him at the time. But, uh, I do remember Danny performing with one of the skiffle bands in the street, and, uh, playing a cigar box and dancing and singing. You didn't see him in his home or anything like that? No.
Didn't know him socially. Yeah. I didn't know his name, for that matter.

Yeah. I only became aware of who he was years later when I met him. He may or may not have been a neighbor at that period, that's what I'm getting at. That's right. Whether he lived on Charter Street in the ten hundred block. As I found out later. Yeah. And he's pointed out the house to me where he was born.
Mm-hmm. Stories about it. The old ice house, of course, is true. Anyway, uh, did you ever hear any bands with carnivals?
Yeah.
I don't remember who he was years later when I met him.
He may or may not have been a neighbor at that period, that's what I'm getting at. That's right. Whether he lived on Charter Street in the ten hundred block. As I found out later. Yeah.
And he's pointed out the house to me where he was born. Mm-hmm. Stories about it. The old ice house, of course, is true. Anyway, uh, did you ever hear any bands with carnivals? No.
Of course, the regular, uh, you know, military-type bands, of course, were always with the carnivals. But I don't ever associate any jazz with the carnivals.
Which kind of carnival are we talking about? Oh, I'm talking about Mardi Gras.
Mardi Gras.
Okay.

Oh, well, you mean in the traveling carnivals. Mm-hmm. Of course, I did travel with, uh, with carnivals that belonged to my parents. And, uh, at that time, we did, in fact, have a minstrel show traveling as part of the carnival. And the minstrel show had a pit band that played jazz. Monk Johnson was the leader. Mm-hmm. And, uh, at various times, both Albert Nicholas and Baby Dodds played in that same pit band, and they were both very young. And the only reason I knew that, because I would not have remembered them. Yeah. But, uh, in discussing it many, many years later, the coincidence turned up that we had, in fact, met before under those conditions.
What, uh, was the name of the carnival?

The carnival was called the... there were two units of what was called the Greater Holkamp show. Mm-hmm. And, uh, these toured through the South and Southwest. Um, and we're now talking about, uh, the period from 1920 to 23, roughly. And, uh, of course, I also knew Furry Lewis, uh, quite well, uh, when I was a kid, since he, too, traveled with and performed with the show.
Uh, it didn't... the carnival didn't take the name of your father or family or anything?

Oh, no. No, uh, there were many Holkamp shows, and, uh, they were universally promoted under the name of Holkamp, but they were all private franchises. And so, uh, it was more expedient to use the name of the, uh, Greater Holkamp shows.
Yeah, that's something I knew nothing about. Uh, I never thought of it being a franchise operation in that period, really. Oh, yes. That's right.

There were probably eight or ten Holkamp shows, and they were advertised and promoted, you know, through the channels through which carnivals are promoted. Uh-huh. Holkamp was basically merely a booking agent.
What was your father's name?
My father's name was Lascaux. Oh, no, his first name? Joseph. Joseph, I see.
And, uh, you had an uncle you told me about who was a musical lover.
Yeah.
That's Lu Shen Delaro's Lascaux.
I see.
And did you go to hear music with him?

Uh, no, but he was the one who brought, who bought most of the records that came into the house. Mm-hm. And, uh, uh, of course we had all the early jazz records, largely because of the fact that he knew the musicians himself, and, uh, and I came to know many of the musicians when I was very young. I remember, for example, some social function that went on in the house when I was very young, for which Papa Celestan's band was hired. And, uh, while I don't remember who the individual musicians were, my first recollection of Celestan comes from the time when I was about five years old, during which time he played in the house. Yeah. What about Buddy Bolden? Well, of course, uh, uh, let's see, I guess it was Fred Ramsey that interviewed me on tape about Bolden, and this, uh, involved a trip that I made with my uncle to, uh, Jackson, Louisiana, to the State Mental Hospital. And, uh, as I understood it at the time, I was just twelve years old then, but that he was making an exploratory trip to find out whether Bolden would either be able to perform again or possibly record, I don't know exactly. But, uh, it turned out to be a futile trip, because, uh, I did have the opportunity to see and meet Bolden, but, uh, I believe he was pretty far gone by that time.
Well, was your uncle hiring bands?

I can't really tell you the answer to that. I know that he was involved with musicians a great deal, and, uh, I do know that he had some project afoot where he was considering doing some kind of recording, but, uh, actually, I was not very clear on the subject at the time. You know, kids, uh, don't explore those things quite as much.
You wouldn't be interested?
Not especially.
So you don't remember any conversation with Bolden or anything he had to say?

No, what I remember particularly is that my uncle brought along a cornet or a trumpet, uh, and his object was to put the horn into Bolden's hands and see whether he could do anything with it. And I remember Bolden taking the horn and examining it as though he had never seen one before, and handing it back with, uh, no interest or apparent recognition.
I guess it was just the kind of thing that he didn't matter to him. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Well, what about cotton candy? I don't know why I asked you that.

Well, um, that's how my family got into the carnival business originally. My father, uh, held holds, the basic patents on the machinery that makes cotton candy. And since, uh, they were originally in the sugar and cotton brokerage business, and, uh, my father was fooling around with attempts to devise ways to improve the refining process for sugar. And during the course of this, developed what we call cotton candy. Uh, I don't know how the suggestion was made, but, uh, he proposed originally to take it out with a carnival to find out something about the appeal that it had to the public, uh, under what seemed to be ideal circumstances for it. It was very successful, and in the process of this, he got actually interested in the carnival business itself and began to assimilate various concessions and finally wound up, uh, the franchise and the whole show. So? He's still alive. Mm-hmm. Your father? Yeah. Mm-hmm.
And, uh, where does he live?
He lives in New York. He lives in New York.
He lives in New York. He didn't stay here, huh? No, he left right after I did.
When did you leave? I left when I was fourteen. Fourteen.
Mm-hmm. So, what about you? I left when I was fourteen.
Fourteen. Mm-hmm.
So, what about you?
I left when I was fourteen. Fourteen.
Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm.
So, what about, uh, Jolly Roll Morton? I'm skipping about. Excuse me.

All right. Mm-hmm. Well, I met Jolly Roll Morton the first time, uh, now, let's see, that's gotta be in nineteen thirty-seven, and, or maybe thirty-eight. I don't know, but it was in the winter at that time. Mm-hmm. I was introduced to Jolly Roll by Rhys Dupree, who, uh, claimed to have been, and may well have been, the composer of Shorten and Bread and Dupree Blues. And it was in a, in a hotel called the Douglas Hotel on Broad and Lombard Street in Philadelphia. I had seen Jolly Roll at the Lincoln Theater either that day or the day before, saw the band, and found it singularly unimpressive, and, uh, went backstage, uh, to see somebody. I don't recall who. I passed Jolly Roll in the car. And, uh, we nodded to each other as strangers, and, uh, had no idea who he was. I mean, he had no idea who I was at the time. And, uh, uh, I was in, having a drink with Rhys Dupree in the hotel while he was trying to convince me to join him in, or actually to finance a promotion that he had afoot, or wanted to have afoot. And in the process, Jolly Roll came in, and we were at the, and, uh, the next time I saw him was definitely in 1938, and that was, uh, at the Jungle, and I first went to Washington for the purpose of being a delegate to the Keep America Out of War convention. And I was on a panel there with, uh, Smedley Butler and John Dooley. And, uh, uh, since I knew that Jolly Roll was there, and that he had this place called The Jungle Inn, I went up. And the first night I went up there, uh, it was about 9.30 to 10 o'clock, and nobody was there but Jolly Roll. And, uh, I asked him, is the place open? He says, yeah, it's open. He said, but you wouldn't know it. And, uh, so he sat down and played, and I had a few drinks, and he had a few drinks, and we talked. And, uh, I stayed there until 3 or 3.30 in the morning. Nobody ever did come in. And, uh, I came in the next night and the next night, and then I took to going in there regularly. And, uh, in fact, uh, I began to make regular trips from Philadelphia to Washington, bringing people with me to see him then, and listen to him talk and play the piano. Uh, and that went on over a period of five or six months.
The first time you heard him there was when you were with Reece Dupree?
Oh, he wasn't playing then. He just came in, you know, into the hotel. Yeah, but he was at the theater. He was at the Lincoln Theater.
Did he play with the band or direct him, or what?
No, he played with the band. Uh, it was not a very impressive band. If I'm not mistaken, it was about a twelve-piece orchestra. Uh-huh. And, uh, I found it very dull.
Was he dull? Do you remember him at all?

No, I don't. Actually, I remember him sitting there and playing. Uh, I don't remember at first that he was especially audible. Yeah. That's one thing in that context. And another thing, uh, uh, I wasn't predisposed to pay close attention to him at the time, because I didn't have much interest in Jelly Roll Morton then. I didn't appreciate him. I didn't know what he was really doing. Uh, what he was playing was by that time substantially removed from what I thought of as authentic jazz. And, uh, that, as I realize now, was largely the fault of the context in which I heard him. Uh, the, uh, the band was clearly not representative of what I would think of as a Jelly Roll Morton sound.
As compared with the, uh, uh, jungle?
With the Red Hot Pepper. Yeah.
And we'll say as compared with the Jungle Inn, when you went there, what did you hear there?

Oh, well, in the Jungle Inn, uh, of course he was only doing piano solos. He was by himself. And, uh, occasionally he would sing, uh, you never had the feeling that he was singing, uh, for the sake of song, but merely to, to, uh, tell you what the lyrics were. In other words, uh, I didn't have the feeling that he was attempting to perform, but merely to state the lyrics. And, uh, uh, I found, uh, my, my original reaction to the music was that it was quaint. I was really not moved yet. I mean, I, I wasn't up to the appreciation of Jelly Roll, as I, of course I am now. But, uh, I thought of him as being an old hat musician who was important historically, and that it was of some advantage to know something about his background and what he had done. But at that time I felt that the business of jazz had moved far beyond Jelly Roll. It's only now that I realize that it never caught up with. I see.

We only have a little bit of tape left on this reel, but, um, I hate to get involved in an entirely new subject, but, uh, what was your very first recording session that you worked on in any capacity at all?

Well, my first recording session that I worked on in any capacity at all, uh, which is strange, was, uh, uh, on a recording of the Andrew Sisters by Mir Bistachain, which, uh, uh, the first session that I made under my own aegis, as it were, was a record of Dan Burley called Chicken Shack Shuffled, uh, 78, with, uh, Pop Sposter and Danny Barker and Jimmy Archie.
What were you doing with the Andrew Sisters? Uh, should I ask?

Well, all that I was doing is that, uh, somebody asked me to, uh, go up there and help out in the recording booth, because somebody who was supposed to have shown up had not. Mm-hmm. And, uh, that, that was all there was to that. I, I don't claim any, but that's the time, that's when I met Bobby Hackett, who played on that.
And what did they, you, you just were working in the booth, just doing something?
Yeah, I was marking things down with a pencil and paper, keeping some kind of a record of something, but I don't recall exactly what it was. I don't imagine you would have been too impressed.
No.
I was impressed with Hackett.
Yeah. Yeah. But, I mean, the details are doing something like that. Who would remember that? Yeah. Uh.
That was a long time ago. That was like in 1935, I think. Yeah.
What about, uh, Dan Burley? Now you mentioned him.

Well, Dan Burley was a very close friend of mine. He was the editor of the Amsterdam News, which was kind of the official organ of Harlem. And he was a very fine newspaper man and a very interesting Red Party style piano player. And Dan and I used to bum around together and we used to do the Harlem scene consistently, and I had a great personal regard for him.
Did you have any sort of business association with him?

Yeah, we had a lot of little things going together. We promoted some dances together and we did a few concerts together. And, uh, but mostly we bummed around. Yeah. I mean, that was the main... We just had sort of minor deals with him. Mm-hmm.
Well, back to, uh, the actual recording session itself. Uh, how did that go with Burley? Well, very well.

It was, uh, it was a very successful session and, uh, sold well. And because of the fact that I really couldn't be... I found that being involved in the record business was, uh, more demanding than I expected. I, uh, sold the masters to Exclusive, who then reissued them on their label.
Well, but what label were they on originally?

That was called R-K, A-R-K-A-Y. Mm-hmm. And, uh, the, uh, it was just too cumbersome. We made four sides and that was about all. I mean, I really couldn't handle the distribution factors. And I found that I really didn't want to be bothered with it, is what it is.
Were you, uh, did, were you owner of R-K?

Yeah, well, I was, I was actually the owner. But we set up a corporate structure with my then business partner, uh, whose name was Kessler, and we just used the initials of R-K. And, uh, but he was not really involved in it at all. I just, uh, had him on as a member of a corporation, because I needed to incorporate.
Well, was there, did you have to call on disc jockeys, or? Yeah.
Yeah. I did all that. Paying all that? Yes, and I found that I didn't care very much for it. So, uh, I discovered how Simi, that side of the record business was, and I just got out of it.
Well, what, what did you think of the music as far as that's concerned? The Burley?
Oh, well, uh, it was pretty interesting. Of course, I was very fond of Dan's playing all the time.
Mm-hmm.

It was a very earthy sound, and, uh, and, uh, extremely indigenous to the, at that time, to the Harlem scene. And, uh, of course, I was always overwhelmed by Pops Foster's bass playing. Yeah. Yeah. And, um, I thought that the rhythm was excellent. Of course, I would not make a record like that today, because I more or less, uh, let Dan have his head in that, and Dan was partial to this saxophone player, John Hardy, who played on a session. Well, played on a session. And I suppose that he was a very good saxophone player, but I discovered, uh, in making that session, that I wasn't really going to be able to make anything successfully that, uh, wasn't actually following out my own musical views. Although, I considered that to be a, uh, an interesting session. Yeah. Looks like you're running out of tape. Yeah, that's what I was just noticing.
I hate to follow along, uh, with the next recording sessions. All right.
Well, we'll make it another time. Yeah.
Well, this is a, a good beginning, and I appreciate it. Okay. I'll have to get out all the appropriate forms for you to sign down.
You'll probably find out a lot of, uh, a lot of things about the music business that nobody ever got near. Yeah.
Well, I guess, uh, not by getting you to sign the forms.
Okay.
Let's let it, one, one second left, I guess. I can't, I can't think of anything that we can cover in that short time. No. No. Mm-hm. Thank you.
I'll go to the second room. Okay.
Al Rose, yeah.
It's your birthday, huh? Yeah, it's my birthday.
How about that?
Happy birthday. Well, thank you.
Yeah. You say that we were talking about Bichet before.

Yeah, we were talking about the first jazz concert. And talking about the people that were there. How well did you know Sidney Bichet? Oh, I knew him very well indeed. Because we made a tour of the Ivy League together, along with Muggsy Spanier and Pops Foster and Baby Dodds and various trombone players. Sometimes George Bruny's, sometimes Brad Gowans. Once later with Jimmy Archie.
You told me a lot of stories about Bichet, none of which come to mind right now.

Well, there are some interesting things. A lot of people that knew Bichet were aware of a period in his life when he got more interested in photography than in music. And I always felt like he was more interested in cameras than taking pictures. He used to come on a job with cameras hanging all over him like a Christmas tree and spend a lot of time shooting pictures of other musicians which never came out. And he was a very mild, quiet type of individual in all of my experience with him. Although he did sometimes become a little impatient with people, but he seemed to mask it well.
Didn't he have women that were bothering him?
Yeah, you don't want me to tell you about Tallulah. Well, that's up to you.
All right.
Well, of course, I've written that for a book. Okay. But Tallulah was just crazy about Sidney and used to chase him around all the time from city to city.
What was his attitude towards Shaker, though?

Well, Sidney really didn't care that much. He was interested in Tallulah, I think, because Tallulah gave him money and gifts of various kinds. And she never seemed to miss an opportunity to find out where he was playing. And, of course, I was always involved to the extent that if they were going to go anyplace together, somebody had to be along to make it look respectable. So I was elected for that.
You were a chaperone.

Kind of a chaperone. Sorry, I find that funny. He was a notorious tightwad. Never spent any money. But one time he did give me a clasp for my necktie, which I eventually gave to Walt Gower, who plays clarinet for the Mother's Boys in Detroit. And he was very reliable on jobs. That is, he was always where he was supposed to be at the time he was supposed to be there. And never seemed to be paying much attention to the other musicians or what they were doing. And was extremely uncritical of other musicians.
How did it happen that he gave you a glass for a necktie?
Oh, we were going someplace, I think it was in Baltimore, and he, in those times it was fashionable to wear these clasps like you're wearing there. I haven't seen one in a long time.
Yes.
And he was wearing one and I wasn't. And he just said, you know, something to the effect that, you look like a slob there. Let me give you something to hold your tie down. And he just put it on.
A tie bar is what I call it.
Tie bar, yeah. Yeah, that's the kind of thing.

And nobody wears them. They wear pins stuck through their ties sometimes. You see that? That's sort of a kind of thing. And of course, the old New Orleans tradition is the diamond stick pin. Whether you have a tie on or not. Well, you still wear a pin yourself, right here in your lapel.
Oh, yeah. That's my Mensa pin. And I don't know. I think I just wear that anymore to remind myself of which suit I had on last. I see.
What's Mensa?

Well, Mensa is an organization of people whose IQs are in the first 2% of the population. And it does not fulfill any of the aims that I hoped it would. And so I haven't been active in it virtually since the time I joined.
Where do they have chapters?
All over the United States. They have a chapter in New Orleans. I've never been to it, but there is one.
You mean there are people in New Orleans?
Yes, there are.
In the 98th percentile.
Yeah, that's right.

About the 98th percentile. Okay. Just checking. I know one thing we were talking about before. We had a slight interruption. I went and gave a lecture. Anyway. We were talking about recording sessions that you had participated in. And we were talking about Dan Burley and then Hardy and that sort of thing.

Yeah. And Danny Barker was on that session too. Yeah. Well, he must have heard several tones. There's another Harry Smith that I've heard of somewhere. Well, did you ever do any recording sessions in New Orleans?

Oh, yeah, of course. Well of course I did a lot of recording sessions in cooperation with Joe Merez. Some of them were mine, some of them were his. And I think I recall that you were present at some of the sessions. I think you were at Woodman of the World Hall when we made the Kingsville Parade with Johnny Wiggs and Raymond Burke and Emil Christian, Jeff Riddick, Paul Barberan, Sherwood Mangiapani.

I came to the Woodman of the World for the dances, and I think I was there for the recording session. I think you were. Those two things get mixed up in my mind. We were talking about that once and how you didn't have the same personnel.
I gave some dances there, that's right, largely in order to set up an opportunity for Johnny Wiggs and people like that to work regularly so that people would have a place to go to hear them.
Incidentally those are still being played on the radio. I still hear that.
Especially at this time of the year. At this time of the year they're still playing.
It saddens me to hear them as a matter of fact. Because so many people are not on the scene anymore.
That's true, but the music is good.
Yeah, the music on the record is good, but what are you going to do to get that kind of sound?

And I believe you were on a session with us when we did that lakefront lounger session at WTPS and we made the Pontchartrain the Beautiful and Spanish capital, you know, old Spanish fortissimo. And of course the records that I make for the state of Louisiana, which are made for the Department of Commerce and Industry, we've made now three LPs there, the third of which will be out within the next few weeks. And we're now planning to do a series of four LPs for the same purpose, except that these will go in the safe to be released as required, but as kind of insurance based on the fact that there are not as many musicians around anymore and that we can't depend on their survival long enough to wait for years in order to record them.
Are there replacements?
Well, there aren't any replacements. Unfortunately that's the case. We're especially weak in piano and drums and clarinet.
And trombone and cornet?

Well we can still manage with trombone and cornet though. There are still some trombone and cornet players. But clarinet players who can play the harmonic role of a clarinet in a jazz band, we don't have. As you recall we found that Eddie Miller was in shape to play clarinet last time, and he hadn't played in thirty years, but he broke out his clarinet and we did make a session. And I don't know what we're going to do exactly next time. I have some plans, enough to cut four more sessions. But we only have the two drummers that are really up to the kind of musical standard that is useful for us now in Sae and Louis Barberan. And we have, of course, Armand Hug and Jeanette Kimball who can play the piano for these purposes, possibly Jeff Riddick. And if Stanley Mendelsohn is in shape we could use him too. And I would like nothing better on this series of four if we could use all four piano players,
and we could use them to play the piano for each session. Well there's a young stuff that plays right, Dan.

You've probably never heard. Steve Pretorius. Well Steve Pretorius is a fine piano player. I did hear him in Sedalia in July at the Scott Joplin Festival. And he's a phenomenal piano player. I think he won fourth prize.
Honorable mention he said, I don't know what that counts for.
He's an extremely good piano player.
I don't know if he's a jazz musician or not.
I don't either.
He's never heard of playing but writing.
I've never discussed it with him.

But before we get too far afield into all the different sessions and what's left today, were you involved in any way with the Brunius Brothers recording or not? No. Nothing to do with it? Not at all. I was just curious, I was listening to that yesterday. It struck me that compared to most clarinet players today, Jules Gala is.
Better than most.
Yeah, he's better than most of them around today.
Sure. I believe, didn't you go out with us to Biloxi one night with Wiggs and Raymond Burke?
I think.
To hear the Brunies band, Abbey Brunies band. I enjoyed that night very much and I was very much impressed by the music.

Well it's funny when you go back and listen to things, you reevaluate them. Oh yeah. And I was interviewing Bill Russell last night and he was talking about the masters that he rejected years ago, so I'm great now.
Oh sure. Well, of course your criteria change and the availability of the quality changes substantially, and of course we just don't have any more like we used to have to work with.
Which sessions did you do with Joe Wiggs?
Joe Wiggs is good, he loved that.
Joe Moritz, who did I insult the most?

Well we did a session with Joe Avery and Louis Barbrun, or Paul Barbrun, excuse me, and a session with Sweet Emma and Percy Humphrey, and of course there was the session that was called Doc and His Patience with the two clarinets, Raymond Burke and Harry Shields, and Jeanette Kimball on piano, and there was also a tuba and a bass on that, Chink Martin and Sherwood and Japanic. Johnny St. Cyril.
What do you think of a soprano sax as an instrument?

Well, I don't think there's much excuse for it actually. It is not bad as a solo instrument, although it's not as true as I like to hear an instrument. But of course there is no place for it in any kind of ensemble. And you know, the fact of the matter is that my own feeling about jazz, I really can't ever really get excited about solos. And to me, a solo or a vocal chorus is more or less an intermission. And it's not that I have anything against them, it's just that that's not the point where I'm listening. I'm always listening for that band sound. And I'd be very happy if you never heard a solo.
Well, a session like Doc and His Patience, you had soprano then, didn't you?
Yeah. There was some soprano, although in some cases they were playing two clarinets.
But you repressed the saxophone play. Oh yeah.

Other than that session, that first session that I made, I never again recorded a saxophone. And any session that I was personally in control of, in charge of, I never used a saxophone. And only on certain occasions did I use saxophones in concerts, and they were for special purposes. Like for example, Bud Freeman worked a couple of sessions for me. But that had a lot to do with the politics of the band, rather than my own musical preference.
Did Bechet play soprano for you?
Well, I was only, I always gave Bechet two or three solos to do in a concert on soprano sax. They were strictly solos with rhythm accompaniments. But at all other times he played the clarinet.
He wasn't hard to control on that or anything? He didn't argue with you? Oh no, no.
There was never a problem with Sidney about programming.
A very agreeable kind of fellow?
Extremely.
Would you call him intelligent in his approach?

I would call him simple and straightforward. He always said what he meant, and you could always get a direct response from Sidney. You knew what he was going to do and what he wasn't going to do, and if he didn't like anything he'd tell you. And there were rarely any kind of situations where I ever saw Sidney having hard feelings about anything with anybody.
But he understood what the music was about.

Oh, he certainly did. He had a very clear concept of what it was about. And he understood the role of his instrument. He also understood the role of the other instruments. And he was frequently frustrated by the fact that the other musicians frequently didn't understand. And I remember one time when I was having lunch, I think it was lunch I was having with Sidney, and Joe Thomas came in who was an excellent trumpet player. And he sat down with us for a while, and I was considering the possibility of asking him to do a concert for me in Philadelphia, but I didn't at that time. But I did take his name, I did take his telephone number. And afterward, when he left, I said to Sidney, how would it sound if we were to get him, because he's a fine trumpet player. And Sidney said, well, he plays the trumpet all right, but he doesn't know any of the stuff that we know, and he wouldn't be able to play with us. So I never did use him for that reason. And the same thing with Frankie Newton. I used to sometimes talk with Sidney to find out what his opinion was of projected concerts that I had. Since he had played with so many of the musicians and knew what they knew, what they were able to play, he could sometimes tell me that.
I find it very difficult to think of many trumpet players that really suited his clarinet playing, specifically I'm speaking.

Well, I found that Max Kaminsky worked out very well with Sidney. And at that time, most of the people that wanted to hear Sidney were really interested in hearing him play Summertime on the fish horn. And we're not very discriminating about bands anyway. It seemed like I was the only one who was worried about the sound of the band. But frequently, and maybe usually, when I hired Sidney for a job, I'd also hire a clarinet player who played mainly the ensemble parts. And it was not uncommon for me to have both Sidney and Albert Nicholas together on jobs.
That worked certainly. Let's see. We were talking about recording sessions. It was Joe Maera- Mm-hm. He worked with him. Were you working for Joe Maera- Mm-hm.

Not really. What was the basis? No. Let me see what would I say was the basis. Joe, as you know, was very much interested in getting the music of New Orleans recorded. recorded. He has a feeling of commitment about it, the fact that there are a lot of musicians who hadn't been recorded or hadn't been recorded properly. And of course I felt the same way about it, and I always thought of myself as helping out, you know, in many cases proposing and producing sessions myself that I thought were suitable. And so there was really a lot of music that Joe didn't know anything about. And I really learned a lot from Joe about the nature of the white jazz musicians' approach, so-called, to the business of jazz. There were a lot of things I never thought about. You know, really it was a long time before I developed any recognition of the competence of most of the white musicians. I probably shared a lot of the prejudices of some of our European friends earlier in my career, and I really tended not to pay too much attention to white musicians. And I think it was Joe and Johnny Wiggs who were able to call my attention to the merits of what they had been doing. And even though I had been using white musicians on concerts, many a time I felt like it was by default, even though I had some great ones. Of course I was kind of overwhelmed by the way Muggsy played lead, and he fit so well into ensemble play, played such a great lead that again, however, I felt like he was just one who had come the closest to the black style, you know. Of course now I understand that there is no black style and it is just New Orleans jazz style, and some people can play it and some can't. How would you fit Bix into that? Well I don't think that Bix would be relevant to any of this. Bix's musical direction was already such that, in my opinion, had he lived and continued to work, that he would have gravitated to the modern sounds. And I hear a lot of Bix and Miles Davis, for example. I may be the only one that does, but I see clearly myself a relationship that goes, you know, from Bix to the moderns, the cool performers. And for my own purposes I trace certain lines. For example, I consider that among the old New Orleans trumpet players that there was already a division in the very beginning, that there were some musicians that were fundamentally good musicians, good jazz people like Oliver and Bunk, you see, and that there were others who were kind of hokum musicians. And I would consider that that would be represented by Freddie Keppert, for example. And I think that most of the genuine, authentic tendencies in New Orleans jazz came down through Oliver and Louis, and that most of the deviations came through Keppert and again through Louis, because there's some of that in Louis too, you know. But branched off into the Eldridge and Gillespie and Gillespie and the Fats Navarro and all those people then. Whereas I see a line, even a separate line, it goes from Bix through Nichols and that period of McPartland's where he was playing that kind of thing. And comes down into people like Chet Baker and eventually the Miles Davises and, in other words, I see three distinct lines of development.
Yeah. Yeah, I'm just wondering how you fit Wiggs into something like this.

Well, how I fit Wiggs in, I think that Wiggs, from a standpoint of band cornet, that is as a jazz band cornetist, is the best jazz band cornetist that I ever heard. That is that he plays better lead, he plays proper lead, makes it easier to put a band together. And you know, to my way of thinking, was the ideal jazz band trumpet player. I also feel that the quality of the music played by Wiggs' bands in the revival is at least as good, and in many cases better, than most of the stuff that we revere as the important collector's items of York. I think from a standpoint of musical quality, that the sessions that Wiggs and Harry Shields and Tom Brown made together are certainly among the very greatest of jazz recordings. I find that I play that stuff more at home than anything else.

Yeah, I find that, in a way, how many, I find this hard to sort out in my mind, because I'm trying to sort out all the different Wiggs's in my mind, and your opinion of the different Wiggs's, our opinions.

Well, of course I always like Wiggs better when he gets the Davenport out of the horn. And I have found that in the right kind of a musical environment he does that. It always seems to me that he plays like Oliver when he's happy and like Bix when he's mad. And I find even that interesting, and I found Bix interesting enough. But, I'm not excited by that, you know, I'm not excited by that. I'm more excited by that, you know, I'm more interested than excited by that. But of course Wiggs, you see, having gone through the original period of jazz, and then gone through the lull, it was possible for somebody like Wiggs to then reassess the whole thing, come to an intellectual understanding of what was happening, and in the process then of putting together music, have a much clearer theoretical understanding of what was happening. Mm-hm. would have. And given all that hindsight then, when you put a band together and you strip away the sentiment of the old time stuff, but base it entirely on the understanding of the music and the ability of the musicians to play their parts, I think that Wiggs put together the best jazz records that I know. Well how do you rate Ray Burke? Well, Rayman is a great creative genius. He is probably one of the most original, certainly the most original creative artist in New Orleans at this time. However, he does not fulfill the classical role of the clarinet in the jazz band, and while he is always a fabulous hand to have on a session, I always feel like you still need a clarinet player if you have Rayman. Somebody still needs to play the clarinet part. I think that I get more kicks from listening to Rayman maybe than any other musician that's now playing. But that's different from structuring
a jazz organization. You could listen to him as a solo I see.

That's right, exactly. And prefer to for that matter. Of course I've recorded Rayman a lot. I had that awful session with Jim Queskin, the jug band musician, a couple of years ago. I never had a chance to hear that for some reason. Well, you haven't missed anything, because this man just is not of the talent caliber to go with the kind of a band that we put together for him. And that was supposed to be released on Warner Brothers, but I doubt whether it was good enough. Not that the jazz men weren't, but certainly the records themselves were not good enough, except for the one jambalaya, which just the band played and he didn't participate in. Of course, Rayman was fabulous on that session. One guy can run a session. Oh, of course, especially when he's the lead singer. Does he play an instrument? Yeah, he plays a guitar. He's all right. He's not a bad guitar player, but what I mean is that when you start putting them together in duets with Emmanuel Sales, that the contrast is marked and he's just not up to that caliber. And it needs just an extremely high-quality musician to be able to play with somebody like Sales. Yeah. What about Naki Parker? How do you fit him into that? Well, Naki Parker is a real musical phenomenon. He is a piano player that gives you an enormous feeling of security when he's working on a session for you. In the first place, his knowledge of material is vast, and his taste is good. He always knows the chords, he always knows the appropriate chords, he's always got a lot of original chords to play, which are original without being outlandish. And he never throws the musicians off, he keeps a good beat, and he's really a superb jazz piano player. I'm delighted with him. I'm also delighted with his interpretive capacity on the ragtime pieces that he does, even though he has his weaknesses because he doesn't practice as much as he ought to. But I really feel that he gets the kind of emotional quality into the rags that they were meant to have. And although I can't demonstrate that, I find that it has a very satisfying quality. His playing has a satisfying quality. How do you know he doesn't practice in that? Does he tell you? Are you lying about that? Well, he tells me, and besides that, you know, I have been with Naki at times when I know for a fact that he hasn't played for several days, and he'll go right on a concert without even warming up and sit right down at the piano and start to play.
What I'm getting at is you all have spent long hours of time together.
Oh yeah, well, Naki was writing his dissertation at my place in Key Largo. He was down there for two months, and Naki virtually never touched the piano in that time, although he had time to do it in.
But some people are compelled to play that. Well, he's not one. Bob Green is compelled,

and he has to get his practice in every day or he gets nervous. And of course, the thing that he's doing is so extremely demanding that I can imagine that it doesn't take much to get out of practice with the business of trying to reproduce literally the sound of Jelly Roll Morton. He works with that variable speed tape recorder, which he regulates the speed of to provide the right pitch. Then he plays the Jelly Roll records, and then he plays the piano, you see. And he's never through until you can only hear one piano. That's pretty exact. Yeah, it's very difficult and very demanding. But of course, he's got that kind of a compulsive personality too, so that he always feels like everything is going to pot if he's not at a piano every day. I'm not sure that's the case.

I've got about one minute. I don't know that we can really get into the things, but we were talking. While we were on these particular people, you had the lakefront lounges there. You had Sherwood, Dr. Bob Barber, Naki, Paul Crawford, there. What do you think of that session?

I think that's a fine session. That's one of the big kicks that I have to recall is the making of that session. It was a pretty freewheeling session, and I felt that we did a lot of very original material there. We had an original approach to things, and I think everybody liked it.
Yeah, I just wondered how it all fit together in your mind with that particular group of people,
if you felt it sounded like an ensemble? I think that it sounded enough like ensemble at the right times to satisfy me. It had a free sound, and I was very, very satisfied with that.
Yeah, well I enjoyed Raymond's solo sound, Tishomingo. Oh yeah. That was a terrific solo, as well as the band playing.
Yeah, I really enjoyed that.
I guess we can call it to a halt now. Okay. It's just the end of the day and the end of the tape. Just about... ... ... ... ... ... ...
